witness_description: Graph on 2 vertices {0,1} with the single edge {0,1}; canonical deterministic DFS (roots and neighbors in ascending order) rooted at 0. Discovery times disc[0]=0, disc[1]=1; tree edges taken in order: [(0,1)]. Take x=1, y=0: y is a neighbor of x and is already visited by the time DFS reaches x (disc[y]=0 < disc[x]=1), yet the edge {x,y}={0,1} IS a tree edge of the DFS - it is exactly the parent edge by which DFS discovered x from y.
refutation_explanation: The claim asserts the implication: if neighbor y is already visited by the time DFS reaches x, then the DFS will not take edge {x,y} as a tree edge. Read literally (the edge is not a tree edge of the DFS forest), this is false: the parent edge of x always satisfies the premise (the parent is discovered strictly before x) while being a tree edge by definition. The minimal witness is the two-vertex path: DFS discovers 0, then takes {0,1} as a tree edge to discover 1; with x=1, y=0 the premise holds but the conclusion fails. Caveat honestly reported by the program: under a stricter 'future' reading - the DFS will not take {x,y} as a tree edge at any moment strictly AFTER x is discovered - the same exhaustive sweep finds 0 violations, so the fragment is presumably sound in its original (unquoted) context where y is an already-finished/ancestor vertex other than x's parent; the quoted text alone does not exclude the parent, and the literal implication is refuted.
search_space: All 75 labeled simple undirected graphs on n = 1..4 vertices (every subset of the C(n,2) possible edges for each n), one canonical deterministic DFS per graph (recursive, roots 0..n-1 in ascending order, neighbors scanned in ascending order), and every ordered adjacent pair (x,y) with disc[y] < disc[x] (205 such pairs). Exact integer arithmetic only; fixed iteration order; first violation in that order reported.
